why does he not think about Canadians, particularly those Canadian researchers who want to get to work in Montreal and other parts of this country?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT OF PATENT ACT-ROLES PLAYED BY MR. PRATT AND MR. HADDAD
speechtext: I say to the Minister that the reason we are preoccupied with what happens in the United States is because the multinational corporations in the United States have drafted Bill C-22. That is why we are concerned.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET MR. HADDAD
REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET MR. HADDAD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the Minister not have the intestinal fortitude to step outside into the foyer to begin some sort of discussions with Mr. Haddad, who is in the Chamber today? Does he not have the intestinal fortitude?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET MR. HADDAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apparently, after some weeks and months of examining Bill C-22, the Hon. Member is not aware that 25 of the 63 companies of PMAC are in fact European. In fact he is apparently not aware that every single one of our industrial partners has been after Canada since 1969 to get in step with the rest of the world and provide the same kind of patent protection provided by the rest of the world.
The Hon. Member may think there is some merit in participation in a debate with an American generic manufacturer. I do not. I think we should get along and do what is right for Canada, in Canada's interest. I wish the Opposition would take the same point of view.

subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to pursue the question of the future of the sugar-beet industry in Manitoba with the Deputy Prime Minister. In an earlier answer the Deputy Prime Minister went on at great length about the commitment of the Government to western Canada. However, many western Canadians know, Winnipegers in particular, that many promises to western Canada have been broken. Why was the promise of the Government to Manitoba and, in particular, to the Government of Manitoba, that no more provincial moneys would be required for the support of the sugar-beet industry, why was that promise to Manitoba, among others, broken?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member would like to outline some of the so-called broken promises because I think this Government has a very distinguished record. I alluded a little earlier to the fact that, out of 52 specific commitments, 43 have been fulfilled and the others are being acted upon.
April 13, 1987

I remind the Hon. Member that we inherited a legacy of high interest, high debt, and high unemployment. We are acting on all three fronts and making progress, I might say, on all three fronts, which is very important to western Canadians-without, I might add, the support of the New Democratic Party.
I can only add, further to my response to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, I tried to respond as best I could and I think I gave an undertaking that, as soon as the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board returns, I will take it up with him and see what can be done. However, I repeat that there was a proposal, as I understand it, put before the Manitoba Government. The Manitoba Government was not prepared to be a party to an agreement, and the Province of Alberta and the Province of Quebec were.

subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not have the time under the Standing Orders of the House to go into all the promises made to Winnipeg and to Western Canada which have been broken.

subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext: Name one.

subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext: The VIA Rail shop in Winnipeg, the Manufacturing Technology Centre. I could go on for some time, Mr. Speaker, but you would not let me.

subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext: Where is the CF-18?

subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext: We won't even get into the CF-18.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MANITOBA SUGAR BEET INDUSTRY
speechtext: The Hon. Member will put his question.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. A proposal was made to the Government of Manitoba, a proposal which involved breaking the promise of the Government that no more provincial moneys would be required. That was a promise made in 1985. When will the Government live up to its promise made in 1985? Never mind what the Government of Alberta does. It lets itself be pushed around by the Government, but not the Government of Manitoba. The Government of Manitoba wants the Government to live up to its promises.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OF NATIVE CLAIMS IN YUKON-MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
SETTLEMENT OF NATIVE CLAIMS IN YUKON-MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I would like to direct his attention to Yukon. He will know that in November of 1985, three parties, namely, the Council for Yukon Indians, the Government of Canada and the Government of the Yukon reached something which is known as the "Memorandum of Understanding". This Memorandum of Understanding sets out the guidelines for negotiating and settling native claims in the Yukon.
Why is it that the Council for the Yukon Indians has signed, the Government of the Yukon has signed, but so far the place for the signature of the Government of Canada remains blank? I ask that question because in June of 1986 the all-party Committee on Aboriginal Affairs recommended that this Memorandum of Understanding be signed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: SETTLEMENT OF NATIVE CLAIMS IN YUKON-MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was not carte blanche from the Standing Committee that that be signed. There were some provisions which were made by the Standing Committee so that the memorandum could be signed. Those provisions, as the Hon. Member well knows, have not been met.

subtopic: SETTLEMENT OF NATIVE CLAIMS IN YUKON-MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
speechtext: Well, the Minister knows that the main provision, as outlined in the Minister's response, was that the Coolican Task Force report be responded to by the Government, and that has been done.

Why does the Minister leave the federal negotiator standing waiting in the Yukon without his instructions? When will the Minister get busy and issue the marching orders to that negotiator, incorporate this Memorandum of Understanding in the mandate, and allow him to get down to work in this important matter in the Yukon Territory?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also recognize, as the Hon. Member does, that the settlement of land claims in Yukon not just for Indian people but for all Yukoners is a very important matter. The mandate is proceeding through Cabinet with respect to the Dene-Metis claim. The CYI claim will proceed. I have already had discussions and will be having further discussions with the Council of Yukon Indians. In due course the mandate will be put forward.
I remind the Hon. Member that there was a mandate in place for over a dozen years. I ask the Hon. Member to allow the Government, which has had from December, to come forward with a mandate sometime this spring, a mandate which we hope will provide settlement of the Yukon claims.

April 13, 1987
Oral Questions THE ADMINISTRATION

subtopic: CODE OF CONDUCT-MORTGAGE ON OTTAWA PROPERTIES- MINISTER'S ALLEGED ROLE
CODE OF CONDUCT-MORTGAGE ON OTTAWA PROPERTIES- MINISTER'S ALLEGED ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister regarding the Code of Conduct and conflict of interest guidelines for Ministers of the Crown. Is the Deputy Prime Minister aware that on February 18 of this year the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport gave a $354,000 subordinated mortgage loan on two investment properties in downtown Ottawa at 494 and 504 Albert Street which are currently the subject of a controversial redevelopment application now before City Hall, and that on the same day he filed a statement with the official responsible for the Code of Conduct which makes no reference to this $354,000 mortgage and gives no indication that it was handled through a blind trust?
In view of the risky nature of this investment can the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House whether speculative commercial mortgage lending is a permitted activity under the Government's Code of Conduct for Ministers of the Crown?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CODE OF CONDUCT-MORTGAGE ON OTTAWA PROPERTIES- MINISTER'S ALLEGED ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity to look into this issue briefly. I am advised, and I would like to inform the House, that the Minister had a 50 per cent interest in this building. It was sold. An interim mortgage has been arranged until August. However, the transaction for the sale has been completed. When the full payment is made in August the Minister will have no further interest in the building in question.
I do not think that this is a matter of hiding anything. Everything has been revealed to the ADRG. My understanding is that this particular transaction is fully consistent with the rules that have been outlined and that the Minister has complied with the spirit of the letter of the rules.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would remind the Deputy Prime Minister of the section of the code that specifically tells cabinet Ministers that outside of their official duties they must not actively manage or operate a business or commercial activity. While I appreciate the Minister's answer he must also be aware-and perhaps he is not-that the properties in question appear to be grossly overmortgaged, except in light of a speculative effort by the new owners to redevelop them.
When a cabinet Minister makes a $354,000 second or third mortgage loan, is that not a commercial activity which is in fact prohibited by the code? What action does the Government intend to take to enforce the code with respect to the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister declared his interest. He has turned around and sold
the property. The corresponding notification has been put in place. As I said, I have looked into this matter in a preliminary way. I am advised that he is complying. But I will check further again and get back to the Hon. Member. I think that the Minister himself may wish to comment on the matter and raise it in the House himself when he returns.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) had the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock 1 was reminding the House that in his budget address the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stressed that all regions in the country were important to national prosperity, and I agree. He said that those regions which depended upon the resource sector were in some difficulty. The words he used were that "some regions are hurting". Then the Minister of Finance added that action must be taken to cushion the blow.
I was telling the House at one o'clock that we in northern Ontario, particularly northeastern Ontario where the unemployment rate is approaching 15 per cent-and across northern Ontario the youth unemployment rate is 22 per cent-were still awaiting some cushion against the economic blows we have been receiving. So far there have been no cushions at all. In fact, the Government has been introducing some additional blows. 1 was reminding the House about the 15 per cent export
tax on softwood lumber and about CNRs 3 per cent hike on the shipment of lumber into the American market. All these things were blows, not to mention additional sales and excise taxes. We are still awaiting the cushion, as promised by the Minister of Finance, for the economic blows we have been receiving.
There are regions which are hurting, and those regions are still awaiting some good news from the Minister. In his Budget address the Minister bragged about the number of new jobs which have been created. It is true that new jobs are always being created, but the Minister failed to tell us about the number of jobs which have been lost, which no longer exist.
For example, in a vigorous endeavour to remain competitive we in northern Ontario in the forest products industry have had to introduce major and very expensive new technology. However, we have lost jobs in the process.
Also, the Minister did not tell the House what kind of jobs were being created. He did not tell the House that a very large percentage of jobs, especially those for women, are now simply part-time jobs at the lowest possible wages and without all the usual benefits.
We in northern Ontario have long depended upon government assistance for job creation. We had the program under the previous administration called Canada Works. Under this Government it has been renamed the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a good program.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Canada Works and the Canadian Jobs Strategy are good. They help the region. However, we are noticing that the number of dollars which the Government is allocating for the program is regularly declining and decreasing, so that fewer and fewer dollars are available while unemployment remains unacceptably high and well above the national average.
I should like to remind the House once again about a program for native people, an area of the economy where unemployment is particularly high. In 1984 the Native Economic Development Program was announced. It was to spend $345 million over four years in order to assist native people to cease being the recipients of social assistance and be able to have economic development programs which would make them self-sufficient.
Since that time only a fraction of the amount of money approved by Parliament has been consistently spent year by year. For example, in 1984-85, the first year of the present administration, Parliament approved $110 million for that program. Out of that $110 million, $102 million was allowed to lapse and only $8 million was spent. Obviously the Government is not even carrying out the will of the House in respect of where unemployment is highest, where people are suffering the most, where people are relying upon social assistance, hand-outs, and welfare, and where there is an opportunity for economic development. The Government allows a substantial
April 13, 1987

amount of money to lapse, and the people continue to be in the same state as they were before.
The point I want to emphasize in conclusion is that we agree with what the Minister of Finance said, that all regions of the country are important to our prosperity, that some regions are hurting, and that this blow needs to be cushioned. However, so far we in northern Ontario have been waiting patiently for a cushioning of those blows. We have been promised a northern Ontario recovery package, and nowhere do we get the details. There has been no action at all to date on what constitutes the northern Ontario recovery package.
Coming out of a meeting in Sudbury, the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) once said to the news media, or is reported to have said, "This statement had better be something more than philosophical in nature; it better have substance". I have urged the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mazankowski) who announced the program to give us the details. Week after week I have asked, and so far I have received nothing, only silence. I want to know when we will get what the Minister of Finance promised-a cushioning of the economic blows in regions like northern Ontario, which is hurting very badly.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) for his excellent speech. To us he is always the person with heart, the man who puts his region or constituency in first place and knows best how to present problems in a very concise and understandable way. I have a question for the Hon. Member on regional development, to which he alluded.
The regional development envelope has decreased by $3 billion since the Government took over in 1984. That is alarming, Mr. Speaker. The concept of Canada from the east to the west and the development of our regions requires very careful and considerate attention. It also has a north-south dimension which is very important. And I know the member agrees with me, that when we talk about Canada we also talk about a mix of the private and public sectors. The Liberal fiscal approach, of encouraging a mix of the private and Government sectors, in certain regions is the only solution.
1 know the member alluded at the end of his speech to the importance of Government participation in regional programs. The privatization program favours high employment centres, mostly in the golden horseshoe and the other highly industrialized sections of our country. When I refer to industrialized sections, we have areas which are not as industrialized as they would wish, areas which are possibly underdeveloped as far as industrial capacity is concerned. Does the Member for Cochrane-Superior not feel that this reduction of the envelope by $3 billion in less than three years has had a very direct serious impact on his area of northern Ontario?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I detected that there were actually two questions posed by the Hon. Member for
The Budget-Mr. Penner
Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). Before one o'clock I had talked about the decline in actual dollars in the regional development envelope. The decline is very serious. If you look at the Estimates you will find about a $3 billion decline which has been consistent since 1984-85.
As well, there is a cumulative effect. We have noticed in northern Ontario that for initiatives of various kinds, and we used to look to the regional development program for assistance, those dollars are no longer available. Some economists looking at our region have said that we really have to forget about having so much emphasis on big industry, on our forest sector, which is in some difficulty, to which I alluded, and on mining, which is in some difficulty because of depressed base metal prices throughout the world. The only exception is gold. I am grateful that we do have the Hemlo gold fields in the constituency of Cochrane-Superior, which is the one bright aspect, economically speaking. Economists have said that we are not looking at the existing possibilities for tourism in our magnificent region. We should be promoting tourism.
I am glad my whip asked me the question because I am going to extend an invitation to him in the next several weeks to join me on a fishing trip. If the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) behaves himself, I may even let him come along as well. I am inviting the Whip on a fishing trip and I will show him how great is the potential for tourism.
Here was a chance for the Minister of Finance in his Budget to have done something to encourage tourism in a region like northern Ontario. He could have said, "Yes, we want to encourage it". But what did he do? The Finance Minister added another 1 cent a litre to the price of gasoline; in addition to the previous 3 cents a litre we had in the last Budget. We have had a total of an extra 4 cents a litre or an extra 18 cents a gallon put on the price of gas when we already had the highest gasoline prices of any of the provinces of Canada. It is true that prices are higher in the far north. So, how is that an incentive for people who want to have a Canadian holiday somewhere in the great Canadian Shield? It is a disincentive.
If you want to fly on one of the charters at one of the main airports to a remote area for fishing-on a scheduled flight- you are stuck with another $4 on top of the ticket price. That is the contribution of the Minister of Finance to the encouragement of tourism in northern Ontario.
I repeat my theme once again. It is a simple one. We agree entirely with the Minister that some regions of this country are hurting, that the blow ought to be cushioned, but he gave us nothing at all to cushion the blow except a lot of sympathy, a lot of understanding, a lot of goodwill and many promises. But so far, Mr. Speaker, nothing in the way of action.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to conclude by saying that the Minister of Finance did brag in his speech that we should all take satisfaction from the fact that the rate of inflation at least is down to 4 per cent, and isn't that something we can all be happy with because now we have more money to spend? But what he did not tell us is that the rate of inflation was the highest of any of the G-7 countries. He did not tell us that of that 4 per cent increase in the inflation rate, two to three points are directly due to the tax burden he has imposed on the citizens of Canada.
He argues in his speech that Canadians now have more disposable income. He does not say that Canadians, since he became the Minister of Finance, have been faced with a 52 per cent increase in their taxes. I am talking about the average Canadian family. The argument about the inflation rate being to the benefit of Canadians is also hollow.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoy hearing from the Opposition with respect to this rather good Budget of February 18. Indeed, comments right across the country have been about the quality of the Budget and the competent administration of our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). I can only say that while the Opposition may not see any good news in the Budget, it was a Budget of a responsible Government.
The Budget indicated that our deficit in relation to the Gross National Product is down 39 per cent, our borrowing requirements in relation to the Gross National Product are down 42 per cent. The Fiscal Monitor issued March, 1987, followed up on the Budget, and I will read from three paragraphs:
For the first nine months of fiscal year 1986-87, (April to December), the budgetary deficit stood at $20.6 billion, down $3.5 billion from the level registered in the first three-quarters of fiscal year 1985-86. The year-over-year improvement in deficit continues to reflect the growth in the economy, restraint on spending and the impact, and timing of past budget measures- financial requirements, excluding foreign exchange transactions, were down $8.8 billion compared to the same period a year ago-total financial requirements, including foreign exchange requirements, stood at $18.2 billion, down $6.4 billion from that registered in the first three-quarters of 1985-86.
That is remarkable management, and it ought to be acknowledged by the other side as remarkable. The harping we have heard is not proper or fair.
We have not had an easy time in Canada during the last year or year and a half. We have seen oil prices decline from $32 a barrel down as low as $10 a barrel, at one point, and I am talking of American dollars. That resulted in a loss of some $1.5 billion in tax revenue from oil companies. It also resulted in a great-retraction in the drilling activities of the oil industry.
It has not been easy in the oil fields, and it has not been easy in the mines. Copper prices are lower than they have been since the Great Depression. Lead, nickel and zinc prices are down to almost unbelievably low levels. The grain trade, not only in wheat but in other grains, is faced with massive competition throughout the world. The effect has been that we have had to sell grains at a world price far below that which should reasonably be expected for the products. As a result, things have not been easy.
I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians have always been described as hewers of wood and drawers of water. Our wood and our water-our raw resources, our soil, timber lands and mines-have not been producing the returns they should have produced, the returns we could normally have expected. Despite that terrible performance in the resource sector and the commodity sector, the GNP has managed to increase over 3 per cent. Indeed, the growth rate was in excess of that of any other country in the OECD, and that is a remarkable performance. That remarkable performance ought to be congratulated by Hon. Members on the other side.
Our remarkable performance has been recognized by the exchange rate. The value of the Canadian dollar has increased significantly since the first of the year. Our remarkable performance can be demonstrated by the interest rates which are down to 1972 and 1973 levels. Over 200,000 homes will be built this year alone. That is remarkable. Yet we hear Hon. Members from the other side grouse, put Canada down and say how terrible things are.
It has been tough in parts of the country. It has been hard in parts of the country that rely on resources and there is a significant unemployment rate in some of those areas. That is a problem we will have to address, but we recognize the problem and we are getting at it. That is why the Government just recently committed $350 million to Alberta's oil industry. That is why the Government spent $1 billion of its funds trying to reinvigorate and help farmers in the production of grains. We are not doing nothing about the situation; we are in fact acting to try to ameliorate the problem in the commodity market and in those parts of the country where growth has not been up to snuff.
Hopefully international markets will improve. It is not the fault of the Government, however, that international markets are soft. The Government is doing what it can to ameliorate the problems of soft markets, but that is all it can do. We will try to do what we can to improve conditions, but conditions cannot be improved by government action alone. We need new international agreements on resources so that countries do not continue to compete with each other by giving away their heritages.
I would like to speak for a moment about the reforms of the House of Commons because I think those reforms are important to Parliament and I think the Budget debate should emphasize those important reforms. I am particularly
April 13, 1987

impressed with the way the committee system has operated. It has given Parliamentarians a better handle on how Ministries are operated.
It is important that we as Members of Parliament exercise our review function and exercise it more diligently. It is important that we examine and cross-examine Ministers and their officials on how they are performing their jobs. Surely when a Government is the size that it is, and represents the invasion into the lives of individuals that it does, it is imperative that we as representatives of the people cross-examine those officials to ensure that the programs they are supposed to be delivering are giving us full value for the money expended. Where those programs are not giving full value, we must as sensible Members of Parliament suggest the removal of, or change in those programs so that Canadians get full value for their tax dollars.
In that respect, may I commend the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) for the way she has conducted the Public Accounts Committee, and members of other committees that have tried to find out how programs are carried out and administered.
I think it is also important that the Government continue to do the things it has been doing in terms of asking directly and indirectly that committees exercise their powers under Standing Order 96(2) to make inquiries into programs and anticipated programs of Government so Members of Parliament will have input before those programs are put into legislation. It is that first look at an idea that gives us as Members of Parliament an advantage. We can have our say in how the country should be governed and how the new activities and thrusts of Government should be put forward.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made an effort to ensure that we as Members of Parliament have the freedom to express ourselves, through the committee system in particular. However, we ought to take a look at the other rules of the House. For the last week the House has been stalemated by one procedural motion after another. In Great Britain, a debate on a complicated piece of legislation can be finished in one day's sitting. There is no reason for delaying and delaying pieces of legislation that are brought before the House, particularly when there is provision for a committee system to allow in-depth analysis of the problems envisaged in Bills and procedures.
The House must reform its rules on debate. We cannot allow important pieces of legislation to be held up while a war takes place across the aisle over whether or not a piece of legislation demanded by the Government is essential. Surely to goodness the voters will eventually decide that; surely to goodness the whole country should not be held for ransom because of procedural delays.
From the point of view of the Finance Committee, it is essential that the Government get ahead with Bill C-42. That Bill deals with combining the Inspector General's office and
The Budget-Mr. Blenkarn
the office of the Superintendent of Insurance. That recommendation was made by the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs a year and a half ago, and it is essential that it be implemented.
Included in that Bill are powers to be given to the new office of the Superintendent of Insurance so that he may discipline and keep in line the trust companies, banks and insurance companies under the aegis of his powers. With some of the things that are happening in the real estate market, particularly in the greater Toronto area, I think it is essential that the Superintendent of Insurance have those powers contained in that Bill. Yet while the House debates Bill C-22 and holds it back, we cannot get at that important piece of legislation.
It is important that before the end of June the House come to the realization that we require rules of procedure that will enable matters to come to a vote, and come to a vote quickly. We cannot be held up any longer by delays and delays. It is bad for Parliament and it is bad for the democratic process, and in a country that is supposed to be progressive and able to come to grips with problems quickly, the causing of one procedural delay after another makes a mockery of democracy.
I would like to deal with the very important matter of tax reform. Our Income Tax Act is unbelievably complex. It is so complex that even leading chartered accountants have indicated that they themselves cannot understand the provisions and ramifications of it. Mr. Don Hugget appeared before the Finance Committee and, addressing me as chairman said, "I cannot understand the Act myself'. He indicated that he had to have someone else help him with his own income tax return.
Tax returns are complicated so badly that despite every effort by Revenue Canada to produce a simplified and easily read form, Dian Cohen indicated the other day on Canada AM that before people even attempt to fill in their income tax returns they ought to buy one of several books which she recommended on how to fill out tax forms.
The Income Tax Act, which contains at least 100 separate allowances, deductions and provisions of benefit in one form or another, creates such complexity that the fairness in allowing these various deductions and allowances is lost. When average people read on their tax forms, "deductions, other", they wonder whether they are getting the benefit to which they are entitled in the tax system. When people believe a tax system is unfair, it is unfair. Because it is unfair it must be simplified to the point where reasonable people with reasonable intelligence can file their tax returns.
To that extent you may recall that last June the Finance Committee filed a substantial report on tax simplification. It is our hope and indeed our requirement that the tax reform package contain provisions of simplification to make the filing of a tax return far easier than it is today. It should be simple

April 13, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Blenkarn
enough that ordinary people can complete their tax return without any professional assistance. That is not the case today and it must be one of the prime requirements of tax reform.
Not only does the present system seem unfair to individuals, but indeed it may well be unfair in itself. The New Democratic Members of Parliament have suggested that certain companies do not pay tax. To some extent they are right. Companies do not pay tax if they are not taxable. When the insurance industry was before the Finance Committee we asked why it did not pay tax. When the trust companies were before the committee we asked why they did not pay tax. When the banks were before us we asked why they did not pay tax. We asked the big real estate developers why they did not pay tax.
They do not pay tax because the present rules are such that they are not taxable. If they are not taxable, they ought to be taxable. The tax reform package ought to make them taxable. I expect that the reform package as presented by the Government will in fact make them taxable so that the unfairness complained of by the other side will no longer exist and Canadians will no longer believe that they are not being treated with the elementary justice to which they are entitled.
Through tax reform, provision should be made for married couples to file joint returns. I believe that all of the attribution rules presently in the system which allow for the transfer of deductions and income from one to another ought to be disposed of. Those are an exceptionally complicated series of provisions. A provision for joint returns would greatly simplify this.
The most important element of tax reform is to ensure that those people who live in poverty, who earn less than the minimum required to put bread and salt on the table, do not pay income tax. That, surely, must be one of the principal thrusts of tax reform. The tax system must reduce tax rates for the poor and lower income people while reducing the over-all personal rate. The over-all personal rate in itself discourages legitimate investment activity. In the current income tax system we have high rates and a whole series of fool deductions. If you take advantage of the deductions you can wind up with a very low rate. Surely we can get rid of the deductions and have a median rate ensuring that everyone pays a fair share. We can have two or three gradations to simplify matters rather than having 14 or 16 different levels. Such a method of taxation would ensure that people are not forever trying to find loopholes or hideaways in the Income Tax Act in order to pay less tax.
I think it is essential that we have a new sales tax system. We cannot continue with the present system which deliberately bonuses importers and deliberately penalizes exporters. If a business transfer tax can be organized to do that, I believe that would be the best form of taxation to have. I hope that when the Government presents its tax reform it will deal with a business transfer tax on goods in order to get rid of the horrendously complicated and unfair sales tax system we presently have to ensure that we come to grips with the problem of imports and exports.
Finally, I think it is important that we deal with capital gains tax. I think all capital gains ought to be tax free, but very few things ought to be considered as capital gains. A capital gain is a long-term gain made by a farmer on his farm over a lifetime, made by a homeowner over a long period of time, or made by someone who started a business, ran it for most of his life, and then sold it. It is not a short-term trade in commodity futures.
That is the kind of thing which is considered a capital gain today and that ought to be fully taxable. A capital gain is not the profit on a strip bond. That is income and ought to be taxed at full rates. We should have capital gains relief for true capital gains and taxation for true income. Activities in the nature of trade are true income, not capital gains, and ought to be taxed at full rates.
I note that my time is up. I would like to speak longer. However, I would like to say that this is a good Budget, and the tax reform promises to be a good tax reform.

I want to make sure that I understood what the Hon. Member just said about capital gains. It seemed rather new, coming from the Hon. Member who fought for total exemption of capital gains. Member gave, as an example of true capital gain, the farmer who inherited a farm from his father 25 or 30 years ago and sells it to his son or another individual. What happens if that same person kept the farm for five years? Is capital gains determined by time or another mechanism? I would be interested to hear more of what the Hon. Member had in mind.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Income Tax Act could have a series of rules built in that would indicate what is a capital gain and what is income. It seems to me that the prejudice ought to be in favour of income as opposed to gain. It would seem, then, that a gain made in less than five years ought to be presumed an income gain, unless the taxpayer can prove to the contrary. It would seem to me that a gain made in over five years ought to be a capital transaction, unless the Government can prove to the contrary.
It would seem, though, that with certain transactions involving the market, such as the strip bond where the built-in gain already exists, that clearly is a situation where money was put up to buy a defined fixed return. That is a designed return on a particular asset over a particular period of time. Transactions such as that which now pass as capital gain ought to be treated as income.
April 13, 1987

However, the general theory is that there ought to be a reverse burden of proof on a period of time. Determining what period is fair or unfair is another matter, but surely that ought to be the theory behind what I am talking about.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be possible to design a mechanism in that respect. After listening to the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), I feel that he is increasingly becoming a red Tory. We are not used to that.
I am very interested in his proposal to eliminate from the tax roll all those who are under the poverty line, although he has not defined what the poverty line is. Would he accept the definition of the poverty line given by Statistics Canada, or does he have another definition of the poverty line?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) is absolutely right. It is difficult to determine what is the poverty line. A number of people have indicated the poverty line as being $8,000 on a single basis and $12,000 for those who are married without children. It is difficult in a country like Canada to define poverty. What is a poverty situation in some parts of Ontario, for example, is affluence in other parts. For example, the poverty line in Mississauga would be very much higher than those figures, whereas the poverty line near my cottage might be substantially less, simply because it is a trading economy with such things as farm products and so on where cash income is perhaps not as important as income from land and trading.
It is always difficult to determine a poverty line in a country like Canada. I believe we ought to be considering it as something like $8,000 on a single basis, $12,000 for married people without children, and an additional amount for families with children. That is always subject to change and what is fiscally possible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to comment on the suggestion that my colleague, the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), is a red Tory. I am beginning to wonder if the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) is a blue Liberal.
I want to compliment the Hon. Member for Mississauga South because I believe he told the story as it is. He gave credit where credit is due in the Budget while admitting that there are some inequities which must be addressed, hopefully in the upcoming tax reform.
That leads me to my question. In his capacity as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, will he comment on what time frame is required for a Government which came to office in 1984 to deal with all that is happening, especially with respect to something as complex as the tax system? The Liberal Party seems to be very impatient for our tax reform package. The New Democratic Party is also impatient, and I notice that the Leader of the New Democratic Party has been sending requests for financial assistance to his Party so that it can try to bring on this tax reform sooner than it can be done by the Government.
Budget-Mr. Keeper

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Make a donation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will not make a donation, but I will ask the Chairman of the Finance Committee to give us a realistic time frame. One would think that it is not a matter one would jump into without knowing all the answers or fully understanding the questions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tax reform problems are much more difficult in Canada than perhaps in most other countries. We have an income tax system federally and provincially in which the federal Government collects income taxes on a personal basis from nine of the provinces and on a corporate basis from seven of the provinces. Our tax system is generally integrated with the provinces in terms of transfer and so on, which means that it requires a great deal of consultation and effort to work out an equitable system that will return to junior levels of government their appropriate share of revenue while not causing any undue displacement of investment in one part of the country compared to another.
The Government has been working very diligently on this problem. I am sure it would like to have been able to present the full tax reform package in the February Budget. I suppose the work is far more complicated than one would realize at the outset, but I am reasonably convinced that the Government will be able to come forward with an equitable package before the end of the spring. That package will have to be examined by Canadians, and it is essential that Canadians from across the country have their input in that package. To the extent that what the Government suggests will not wash with Canadians, I would think that the Committee on Finance ought to listen to Canadians and be able to come up with recommendations for perhaps even further change.
Tax reform clearly must be a matter of consensus. It must be a matter where no one part of society is unfairly injured. I say "unfairly injured" because some people are perhaps not paying the taxes they should. Some organizations perhaps are not carrying the tax burden they should. However, we must ensure that in asking them to carry a larger tax burden, we do not so upset their activities in the country as to injure the country over-all. It is not an easy matter but it is a matter the Government is dedicated to complete. I am sure the Government will be calling upon all Hon. Members of the House for their co-operation, efforts and energies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to enter into this debate. I must say I have just about forgotten what this Budget is all about. It has been a while since the Budget came before the House and the time of the House has been taken up with other matters. I welcome the fact that we are back on the Budget debate. It needs to be completed. The Budget needs to have the debate that it deserves.
I am also glad that the legislation with regard to generic drugs is not before the House today, because that is an unjust

April 13, 1987
Budget-Mr. Keeper
project the Government has undertaken and to which it has committed itself and the Government should have time to reflect. 1 hope the Government uses the opportunity today to take another look at its attempt to give a sweetheart deal to the pharmaceutical drug companies, thereby taking money out of the pockets of ordinary Canadian consumers, particularly elderly people who have a hard enough time to make their dollars meet their expenses. I hope the Government will use this time to reflect and will find its heart when it has an opportunity to take a look at what it is doing.
As I said, it has been a while since this Budget was presented in this House, and I had to go back and reflect on just what it is all about. After having looked at some of its provisions, I have come to the conclusion that this Budget is a do-nothing Budget. It has no major initiatives. It takes very little action. Therefore, it is very understandable why I had forgotten the contents of the Budget. It is a Budget that shows the Government cares very little about the average Canadian family, about the hardest hit regions and the poor, whether those poor are here in Canada or in the Third World.
I want to elaborate on my conclusions. I want to comment about what I see as the impact of the Budget. What could the Government have done instead of doing nothing? Can we afford to act? Do we have the money to do some of the things that I would like to suggest we should have done? To begin with, I say the Budget is a do-nothing Budget because it does very little or nothing for the average Canadian family. I think we should take note of the fact that over the last couple of years under a Conservative Government, taxes on the ordinary Canadian family have been growing. In fact, over the last couple of years, taxes have risen by some $1,350, so that the average family is now paying $1,350 more a year in taxes than it did two years ago before this Government was elected. Obviously, the majority of Canadians who elected this Government, hoped for much better. They hoped their condition would improve. They hoped to be able to face their financial responsibilities a little better today than a couple of years ago. Canadians are not unrealistic. They do not expect miracles overnight. However, they did expect some improvement in their condition. What in fact they received was a whopping increase in taxes. We might say this was fair if we were able to conclude that everyone had to pay more taxes because we were trying to dig ourselves out of a massive debt hole created by the previous Liberal Government. Obviously, there is a massive debt created by that Government. The argument could be made that it is fair for everyone to pay more taxes because we have to get rid of this debt. But is it fair?
At the same time that the average Canadian family is paying $1,350 a year more in taxes, wealthy Canadians have been given a tax break through changes in the lifetime capital gains exemption. If one owns property, and if that property rises in value to the extent of $.5 million, one would not have to pay taxes on that. Therefore, if one is wealthy, there is a tax break. At the same time, average Canadian families had their
taxes increased. So I contend that it is unfair. I suggest that the average Canadian would consider that an unfair approach to raising revenue. Canadians recognize that in order to have services, they must pay, but they want these services to be paid for in a fair manner, but when they have to pay vastly increased taxes at the same time that wealthy Canadians get a tax write-off, they must conclude that it is unfair.
Another aspect of fairness with regard to taxation in this Budget has to do with those Canadians who live in poverty, which is fully a fifth of the Canadian population. Obviously, we could have some debate about just exactly how many people are poor or how many are not poor, but I think there is a general consensus that at least a fifth of the population could be considered poor, to put the estimates in modest terms. What we note about taxes is that Canada's poorest individuals and families have to pay taxes on incomes of less than half the poverty line. So not only can one be poor living below the poverty line, having less income than it takes to provide for one's own basic human needs, but at the same time one can be asked to pay taxes. Individuals who are really in difficult circumstances are still being asked to pay taxes. It strikes me as unfair to ask people, who are earning less than half of what an income would be if they were at the poverty line, to pay taxes, at the same time that wealthy Canadians who have large capital gains are being told their taxes are forgiven. That is unfair. When a Budget does nothing about that kind of situation, it can justly be called a do-nothing Budget.
Canadians are not only concerned about the poor in Canada. We are concerned about all the poor because we have a sense of justice and compassion. In fact, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was campaigning referred to Canadians' compassion and really sought to gain support from Canadians by indicating that he shared that value. But what have the Conservatives done in the Budget? They have reduced the amount of official development assistance by $150 million this year. They have reduced the amount of aid which goes to the poorer countries in this world. That is unfair. We can all remember the terrible famine that took place in Ethiopia. We can remember the graphic pictures of starving children that we saw on television. Canadians responded to the need. They gave from their own pockets. To give the Government credit, it also responded in those moments. But it is to these types of situations that we have to respond on an ongoing basis. This means that we need to place a higher priority on the assistance we give to the Third World rather than a lower priority. I say "priority" because I think it is possible for Canada to raise the revenue to do the things it needs to do and at the same time to have enough revenue to help globally, to help bring about greater justice in the world.
In fact, what the Government has done through this Budget is to reduce the amount of money that we spend on development assistance. I call that doing nothing since there are changes in policy with regard to development aid that the Government could have undertaken. It could have accepted
April 13, 1987

some of the long-standing recommendations from the development community which calls for aid to be on time. In other words, when we undertake an aid program in a given country, the resources should respond to the priorities of the country rather than to our own priorities in terms of our economic development or in terms of the types of goods our companies sell. It has been well documented that giving aid to another country while tying it to that country's purchasing goods from Canada can distort the aid. Thus we end up not helping the country. While on paper we are claiming to help, in reality we are not helping at all. In fact, we are wasting our own money. If we want to spend money on development aid then we want it to be spent effectively. We want it to result in development. While the Government could have done something in this area in fact it has done nothing.
The Budget has postponed the whole question of tax reform. There is a growing consensus in the country that the tax system is unjust, that it is too complicated, that there are too many loopholes in it and that we have to find a more fair way to raise the revenue we need in order to deliver the services which the Government has the responsibility to deliver, However, the Government has postponed any efforts at tax reform. Rather than bringing forward something with respect to tax reform in this Budget, which was an opportunity for the Government to take action, it chose to do nothing. It chose to put off the day when we will see tax reform. One can speculate as to why it did that. Perhaps it hopes that it can have a tax reform package prepared for the next election and announce it just before it in an attempt to curry public favour, in an attempt to seek to improve its own political fortunes. If I wanted to be cynical about the whole matter I would say that it would announce such proposals at a time approaching the next election but too late to give Canadians an opportunity to experience the impact of such a measure. In this way the average Canadian would have no real way of evaluating the impacts of such measures and whether they really lived up to the promises made. Instead of acting on tax reform, the Budget has further increased taxes on the average Canadian family by $65 to $100 per year.
So taxes have been increased in the Budget, inclusive of taxes on gasoline, airline tickets, cigarettes and snack food. We have all heard of heartless Governments before. However, a Government that increases taxes on children's candy, on granola bars and chocolate bars, is truly heartless. I must say that I try to discourage my children from eating chocolate bars because I know that they are not good for their teeth. I know that sugar can decay teeth. However, I am not always successful in this end and, of course, a child can buy a granola bar rather than a chocolate bar.
Why has the Government chosen to pick on little children while giving tax breaks to wealthy Canadians? It has chosen to impose taxes on snack foods, thus taking candy out of the mouths of babes. That is heartless. While it imposes taxes on children's candy it does nothing in terms of child care. The
Budget-Mr. Keeper
Government postponed action on child care. This is a key area in which there is a growing consensus with respect to the need for action. It is one of the most important areas of public policy in which Governments will be constantly pressured for action until we arrive at a point at which there is adequate child care. Because of demographic changes and because of changes in work habits we need day care in a way that we have yet to face up to. The Government has chosen to tax children's candy and do nothing about child care-
